title: Method `render_template` does not use blueprint specified `template_folder`

messages.content: I am looking at issue #1361 in the Flask repository. It seems that render_template fails to respect the template_folder defined in a Blueprint. When I call render_template inside my blueprint, it looks at the global app templates rather than the blueprint-specific ones. Could this be a bug in how Flask manages the template resolution order?

This is a known limitation in the Flask template engine integration. When you call render_template, it uses the global JINJA_ENV on the Flask application object. By default, Blueprint template folders are added to the global application's template search path when the blueprint is registered, but they are appended to the end of the list. If you have duplicate filenames like search.html, the app's root templates take precedence.

That explains why the order in the template list matters so much. If I want to isolate the templates to the blueprint, how should I modify my test.py? Should I explicitly prefix the path, or is there a way to configure the Blueprint to force it to look only in its specified template_folder?

Currently, Flask doesn't provide a way to 'isolate' a blueprint's template namespace purely via configuration. One common workaround is to use directory names in your template paths, such as render_template('a/search.html'), but if you want the blueprint to own those files, you might need to look at how we inject paths into the jinja_loader in the Flask source code, specifically inside the setup_template_loader method.

I have been examining flask/templating.py and flask/blueprints.py. It seems the issue is that register_blueprint registers the folder globally instead of creating a scoped loader. If I attempt to modify _get_template_loaders in the Flask class, could I potentially prioritize the blueprint's loader if the request context is within that blueprint?

That is an interesting hypothesis. Modifying _get_template_loaders to inspect the current blueprint associated with the request would be invasive. Remember that Jinja2's Environment is shared across the app. If you change the loader dynamically based on current_app.blueprints, you might run into thread-safety issues or performance regressions since that check would run on every render call.

Good point on the performance hit. What if I explicitly call render_template_string or use a custom Jinja2 loader specifically for the blueprint? Or perhaps I should propose a feature where Blueprints can register a specific prefix for their templates to avoid collisions?

A prefix-based registration is a common design pattern in other frameworks. If we look at the internal implementation of render_template, it simply calls jinja_env.get_template. If you wanted to support this, you'd likely need to update Blueprint.register to attach a custom ChoiceLoader to the application that delegates based on the current context.

Let me try writing a reproduction script using a Mock that simulates the current behavior. I'll define a test case in tests/test_blueprints.py where I register two blueprints with different templates named the same. If the assertion fails, I know I've locked down the bug behavior.

That sounds like a solid plan. Make sure you use the Flask test client. Initialize the app in your test_blueprints.py, register the blueprints with their respective template_folder arguments, and assert that hitting the route returns the content specific to the blueprint rather than the root directory content.

The test failed as expected! It returned the template from the root templates/ folder. I'm digging into flask/templating.py now. I noticed that the app object builds a list of loaders. Maybe I can inject the Blueprint template loader higher up in that list?

Exactly. Inside the Flask initialization or the registration phase, the template loader is constructed. If you verify the order in which the loader list is populated during app.register_blueprint, you might find that you can reorder the list so that blueprint-specific folders appear before the root template folder.

I found that the blueprints' templates are appended to the list in flask/app.py via a call to _add_template_folder. If I change that logic to insert at index 0, it might work, but that would give all blueprints highest priority. That might be too aggressive, right?

That's correct. Inserting at index 0 would make the blueprint's templates override *everything*, even the application's own templates. That would definitely break existing functionality for developers who expect app templates to act as overrides or defaults.

What if I implement a custom loader that checks for the existence of the template in the blueprint path before falling back to the default? I can create a custom loader class that wraps the existing loader logic.

That is a much cleaner architectural approach. Implementing a custom Jinja2 loader that handles path resolution logic allows you to maintain the current loading sequence while adding your lookup logic. You could use this to resolve templates against the specific blueprint registered in the app's blueprint dictionary.

Okay, I'm prototyping this custom loader. I'll need to use request.blueprint to know which blueprint is active. Wait, what if the template is rendered outside of a request context? I need to handle that gracefully, perhaps by falling back to the standard loader.

Yes, always check if current_app.got_request_exception or if there is an active RequestContext. If you are rendering in a CLI context or during app startup, you won't have a blueprint-scoped context. Your loader should check for has_request_context() first.

The prototype works in my test suite! I'm now cleaning up the code to ensure it complies with the existing Flask coding standards. I'll include the new loader in flask/templating.py and update the Blueprint registration flow.

Excellent work. Ensure you add comprehensive unit tests to tests/test_blueprints.py that cover both the collision scenario and the standard rendering case. Once you're finished, consider opening a Pull Request against the Flask repository with your changes to flask/templating.py.

I've hit a snag with the tests/test_blueprints.py implementation. The current tests don't simulate a nested blueprint context well enough to trigger the specific TemplateNotFound error I'm trying to solve. Should I be mocking the Jinja2 Environment within the flask/templating.py test suite?

Mocking the Jinja2 environment is a slippery slope. Instead, I suggest using the Flask test client to push a context. You can use app.test_request_context() and then manually set the request.blueprint attribute to simulate the blueprint resolution before calling render_template.

That makes sense. I just updated the test helper in tests/test_blueprints.py to use app.test_request_context('/test'). It successfully simulates the blueprint context, and my custom loader in flask/templating.py is now correctly identifying the template folder from the registered blueprint.

Great, does the loader successfully fallback to the main template folder when the template isn't present in the blueprint's directory? We need to ensure we aren't losing the ability to access base templates.

It handles the fallback correctly! I implemented a try-except block inside the custom loader's get_source method. If the file is not found in the blueprint's directory, it calls the super().get_source() method to look in the application's root template folder.

That seems robust. However, look closely at flask/templating.py—does this impact the performance of every template look-up? Adding extra file system checks might be expensive for large projects. Have you considered adding a simple internal cache?

Good point. I'll add a small dictionary-based cache to the loader instance. I should use the (blueprint_name, template_path) tuple as a key. I'll need to make sure this cache is invalidated if the blueprint's template_folder changes, though that's rare.

Sounds like a solid optimization. Remember to define that cache attribute in the __init__ method of your loader class in flask/templating.py to avoid shared state issues across different application instances.

I've implemented the cache. Running the full test suite now: tests/test_blueprints.py and tests/test_templating.py. Wait, I'm getting an AssertionError in tests/test_templating.py. It seems the Jinja2 environment's loader is now nested differently than expected.

The Jinja2 loader hierarchy can be tricky. When you wrap the loader, make sure the Environment object still points to your new instance. Check flask/templating.py again—did you accidentally double-wrap the loader?
You nailed it. I was calling _get_jinja_loader multiple times in the app factory. I fixed it to ensure the custom loader is instantiated exactly once. The tests are green again!

Excellent. Now, how are you handling the case where a user has multiple blueprints with the same template filename but different template folders? Does the current resolution order respect the registration order?

Yes, because the active blueprint is identified by the RequestContext. Since a request is tied to one specific blueprint's route, it shouldn't conflict with other blueprints. It only looks at the currently active blueprint's folder.

That sounds correct. Since render_template relies on the request context to determine which blueprint is active, there shouldn't be any leakage between blueprints. Have you checked if this affects 'url_for' or other blueprint-aware helpers?

I haven't explicitly checked 'url_for', but those logic flows are separate. They rely on the blueprint's static_folder or URL prefix, not the template loader. I think the changes are safely isolated to templating.
Agreed. One last thing: make sure you update the documentation string in flask/templating.py for your custom loader class. It's crucial for maintainability.
Adding the docstrings now. I've documented the lookup order and the caching behavior. I'm also adding a note about the fallback mechanism for maintainers.
Perfect. Once you're done, perform a final linting check. Ensure there are no PEP 8 violations in flask/templating.py or your new test cases in tests/test_blueprints.py.
Running flake8 now... everything looks clean. No violations. I'm ready to commit these changes to my local branch and prepare the PR. Thanks for the guidance on the loader architecture!
You're very welcome! This architectural improvement will significantly improve the usability of blueprint template folders. Good luck with the PR submission.

I've pushed the commits. Actually, I noticed an edge case while testing against a production-like environment: if I use 'render_template' outside of a request context, my custom loader in 'flask/templating.py' raises an 'AttributeError' because 'flask.globals._request_ctx_stack' is empty. How should I handle this gracefully?

That is a great catch. Using 'render_template' outside of a request context is common in CLI tasks or background jobs. You should implement a fallback check: verify if the request context exists before attempting to access the active blueprint. If it's missing, you should default to the standard application-level template loader.

That makes sense. I can wrap the loader lookup in a conditional. In 'flask/templating.py', inside '_get_jinja_loader', I'll add an 'if _request_ctx_stack.top is not None' check. If that evaluates to false, it should just return the default 'app.jinja_loader'.

Exactly. Ensure that your logic inside 'flask/templating.py' doesn't create a circular dependency. Since you are touching 'flask.globals', be careful about how you import it to maintain compatibility with older Flask versions if that's a requirement.

Good call. I'm currently using 'from flask.globals import _request_ctx_stack'. I'll test this with a dummy test script in 'tests/test_blueprints.py' that calls 'render_template' from a 'with app.app_context():' block, which obviously won't have a request context. This should verify the fix.

Sounds like a solid plan. Have you considered what happens if the user manually specifies a template search path that includes the same filename in both the app and the blueprint? The fallback might become ambiguous.

If a developer manually provides a path, I'm setting the blueprint-specific folder to have higher priority in the 'ChoiceLoader'. I think that's the expected behavior. If it falls back to the app loader, the app-level templates are naturally lower priority than the blueprint's override.

That logic holds. Make sure to run 'pytest tests/test_blueprints.py' after this change to ensure the behavior is explicitly verified and covered by the test suite. Regression testing for the app context is critical here.

Running the tests now. Uh oh, 'test_render_template_outside_request' is failing. It seems I am still getting an error when accessing the blueprint name from the context, even with the guard clause. Let me debug the stack trace.

Check your 'flask/templating.py' again. Is it possible that the code is reaching the blueprint resolution logic before the guard clause? Print out the stack trace and verify exactly which line throws the exception.

You were right. I put the guard clause after the lookup. Moving the guard clause to the very top of '_get_jinja_loader' resolved the 'AttributeError'. Now the tests are passing, and it correctly falls back to app templates.
Excellent. Now that the context issues are resolved, have you verified if this change impacts memory usage with the Jinja environment? Multiple blueprints might create redundant loader instances.

The 'ChoiceLoader' is memoized, so redundant instances shouldn't be an issue. Each blueprint should only trigger a single loader instantiation per request cycle. I've double-checked the memory footprint, and it looks stable.

Glad to hear it. Are there any edge cases regarding template inheritance? If a template in a blueprint uses '{% extends "base.html" %}', does it correctly find the base in the app's 'templates/' directory?

Yes, because the 'ChoiceLoader' contains both the blueprint's folder and the app's folder. When Jinja tries to resolve 'base.html', it iterates through the list in the 'ChoiceLoader'. It will check the blueprint, then fall back to the app root.
Perfect, that is the desired behavior for standard template overrides. Are you confident in your current test coverage in 'tests/test_blueprints.py'?

I have added four new test cases: one for standard rendering, one for blueprint path overrides, one for the app context fallback, and one for nested template inheritance. I believe that covers the primary critical paths.
That sounds comprehensive. Before you finalize, double-check the 'Flask' object initialization to ensure no side effects occur if a user registers blueprints dynamically at runtime.

I checked 'app.register_blueprint()'. Since the loader is constructed lazily inside the route resolution flow, it should handle dynamic registrations without issues. I'm feeling good about this solution now.
Great work. You've navigated the complexities of the Flask template resolution system well. Submit your PR with the updated test suite, and you should be in good shape for a merge!

I'm reviewing my changes in 'flask/templating.py' one last time before pushing. Wait, what about 'render_template_string'? Does that method utilize the same loader resolution logic as 'render_template'?

Good catch. 'render_template_string' directly processes a provided string through 'jinja_env.from_string'. It does not interface with the file system loader, so it remains unaffected by your changes to 'ChoiceLoader' logic.

That makes sense. I noticed that 'render_template' calls '_get_source_fast', which is where I applied the loader logic. Should I look into 'render_template_string' anyway to see if we can leverage the new loader context there?

Probably not necessary. 'render_template_string' is intended for ad-hoc rendering. If you were to force it through the blueprint loader, it might actually cause confusion for users who expect a clean, isolated template string.

Understood. I'll stick to the current scope. I noticed a subtle issue in 'tests/test_blueprints.py' where the teardown wasn't properly resetting the 'app.jinja_loader'. I should fix that to ensure test isolation.

That's a vital observation. Unchecked state in the 'Flask' object during testing can lead to flaky suites. Ensure you're resetting to the default 'FileSystemLoader' if necessary in the 'teardown_method'.
I implemented a fixture that restores the original 'jinja_loader' state. After running 'pytest tests/test_blueprints.py', all tests passed. The isolation seems much more robust now.
Excellent. Does the test suite now cover the case where a blueprint has no 'template_folder' defined? We should ensure the loader falls back gracefully to the application defaults.
Yes, I added a 'test_blueprint_without_template_folder' case. It asserts that the 'ChoiceLoader' correctly ignores the missing path and defaults to the 'app.root_path' templates.

That confirms the robustness of the implementation. Have you verified how this interacts with the 'template_context_processors'? Those processors often expect access to the global template environment.

The 'template_context_processors' are applied at the 'jinja_env' level, so they persist regardless of the loader modification. I verified this by printing the context keys during rendering; they remain present.
Perfect. It seems you've considered all the peripheral systems. Are you planning to add any documentation comments to 'flask/templating.py' explaining why the 'ChoiceLoader' is constructed this way?
Yes, I'm writing a brief docstring for '_get_jinja_loader' noting the priority of blueprint templates over the global ones. This should help future contributors understand the ordering logic.
That documentation will be invaluable. The internal intricacies of Flask's template lookup are often opaque to newer developers. Is there anything else you want to refactor before finalizing?
I am considering cleaning up the import statements in 'flask/templating.py'. Some of the Jinja imports are quite verbose. Is there a preferred style here?

Generally, keep imports explicit. Avoid 'from jinja2 import *'. If you want to shorten, use 'from jinja2 import ChoiceLoader as JinjaChoiceLoader' to avoid naming conflicts with your internal implementation.
I'll adopt that alias pattern. It makes the code cleaner without sacrificing readability. I've finished the refactoring, and 'flake8' reports no linting errors.
Splendid. You have verified the logic, addressed the state-leakage in tests, documented the behavior, and cleaned up the implementation. You're ready to submit.
Thanks for the guidance. I'll open the pull request against the 'master' branch. I'm feeling confident this resolves the reported issue with blueprint template resolution.
Happy to help. You've handled this with the rigor expected for such a core library. Good luck with the PR review process, and feel free to reach out if issues arise.

Wait, I just had a thought while drafting the PR description. If a blueprint has its template_folder set to a subdirectory, and the user calls render_template with a path that includes that same subdirectory, could we end up with double-loading or redundant paths? Should I add a check in _get_jinja_loader?

That is an excellent point, but typically Jinja's loader handles path normalization quite well. If you check flask/templating.py, you'll see the loader treats the folder as a search root. If the user provides a sub-path, it is relative to that root.

Right, so if the folder is 'templates/a' and the user renders 'a/search.html', it looks for 'templates/a/a/search.html'. That would cause a 404. Is this behavior expected, or should we be stripping the blueprint prefix?
It is expected. Blueprint template folders are designed to provide a sandboxed view of the filesystem. If you strip the prefix, you break the user's explicit intent. It is safer to leave it as-is.
Fair enough. I've updated the docstring in flask/templating.py to clarify that the blueprint's template_folder acts as the root search directory for that blueprint's templates.
That clarification is perfect. It explicitly warns developers about the scoping behavior. Have you run the existing test suite in tests/test_templating.py to ensure no regressions?
Yes, I ran pytest tests/test_templating.py and all 42 tests passed, including the new test case I added for this blueprint resolution issue.
Excellent. Passing the existing suite is the final hurdle. Since you've verified everything, you can push your changes to your fork and submit the PR now.
I'm pushing the branch now. Should I include the full trace of the failure in the PR description, or just a summary?
Include the failure case summary and the 'test.py' snippet you shared earlier. It helps the maintainers quickly reproduce the bug without digging through files.
Done. PR is up: https://github.com/pallets/flask/pull/1361-fix. I'm waiting for the CI build to complete. It triggered the 'tests-linux' suite.
That is standard for the Flask repo. They have a fairly robust CI pipeline. If those pass, you are in great shape for review.
Everything passed! Though, a reviewer just suggested using 'os.path.abspath' for the 'template_folder' path to ensure consistency across different OS environments.
That is a wise suggestion. In flask/templating.py, you might need to import 'os' if it is not already there. It avoids edge cases with relative path resolutions.
Exactly. I'll add the 'os' import and update the setup logic. It's a small change but improves robustness.
It is all about those small, robust details. Once you push that patch, notify the reviewer that you've applied their feedback.
Everything is updated. The reviewer seems satisfied with the 'os.path' usage. Do you think there's any risk with 'os.path.join' vs 'pathlib' here?
For this legacy codebase, 'os.path' is more consistent with existing patterns. Don't worry about 'pathlib' unless they explicitly ask for a modern refactor.
Good call. I will stick to the existing style. Thanks for the guidance during this process; it's been a great learning experience.
It has been a pleasure. You have navigated the Flask architecture and a tricky templating issue successfully. Happy coding!

Wait, before I merge this, I noticed a potential side effect. If someone provides a relative path in 'Blueprint' init, 'os.path.abspath' might resolve against the current working directory instead of the package root. Is that an issue?

That is a great catch. 'Blueprint' is often initialized within a module. You should use 'os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), template_folder))' to anchor it to the blueprint definition file location.

Right, relying on the working directory is flaky. I will adjust the logic in 'flask/blueprints.py' to resolve the path relative to the module's directory. This ensures consistency regardless of where 'start.py' is invoked.
Precisely. This pattern is safer and avoids the common pitfall where 'app.run()' is called from different parent directories, breaking relative template lookups.

I've updated the implementation in 'flask/blueprints.py'. I tested it by moving 'start.py' to a parent directory and running it. The templates are now correctly resolved from the 'templates/a' folder.
Excellent. Testing from different entry points is the best way to verify path resolution logic. Does the 'test_blueprint' still load correctly if the user passes an absolute path?
Yes, I added a conditional check: 'if not os.path.isabs(template_folder):' it joins with the caller's directory. Otherwise, it uses the provided absolute path directly.
That logic is robust. You've handled both edge cases—relative vs. absolute—which makes the API much more predictable for other developers.
Should I add a regression test in 'tests/test_blueprints.py' to cover this specific scenario? It might prevent future regressions if someone touches the 'Blueprint' initialization.
Definitely. A test case that initializes a blueprint with a relative path and verifies 'app.jinja_loader' contains the expected path is standard practice for the Flask project.
I've drafted the test in 'tests/test_blueprints.py' using 'pytest'. I'm mocking the directory structure to ensure the test is isolated and doesn't rely on the actual filesystem layout.
Mocking is perfect here. It prevents 'tests-linux' or other environments from failing due to differences in file system permissions or structure.
The tests pass! I've pushed the changes to the branch. The reviewer just commented that the logic is clean and fits well within the current 'flask/blueprints.py' style.
That is great news. It sounds like your fix is nearing the merge stage. You've successfully navigated the 'template_folder' path resolution issue.
One final check: should I update the documentation in 'docs/blueprints.rst'? Users might not know that absolute paths are now explicitly supported in this way.
Yes, updating the documentation is crucial. Clearly state that 'template_folder' can be an absolute path and how relative paths are resolved. It is a win for user clarity.
I've added a note to 'docs/blueprints.rst' under the 'template_folder' configuration section. It should now be clear to developers how this behaves.
Your PR is looking complete. You have the implementation, the regression test, and the updated documentation. This is high-quality work.
Thanks for the support. I'm hitting the 'Request Review' button again to notify the maintainers about the final doc updates. This feels solid.
You are ready. Best of luck with the final review and merge. It was a pleasure working through this with you!
I noticed in the CI logs that the 'docs/blueprints.rst' changes caused a slight linting warning in 'tools/check-docs.py' regarding line lengths. I should probably clean that up before the merge.
Good catch. 'tools/check-docs.py' is strict about formatting. Wrap the new text in 'docs/blueprints.rst' to comply with the 80-character limit and avoid any unnecessary pipeline noise.

Fixed the line lengths in 'docs/blueprints.rst'. I'm rerunning the doc linting script now to ensure everything is compliant. It's frustrating how easily a simple documentation update can trigger these checks.
It's standard practice in large projects like 'flask' to keep documentation as clean as the source code. It ensures that the rendered HTML output remains consistent and readable.
The linting check in 'tools/check-docs.py' passed! I'm now pushing the doc-fix commit to my branch. Should I squash these into a single clean commit for the reviewer?
Yes, please do. It makes it much easier for the maintainers to review the history. Use 'git rebase -i' to combine your implementation, testing, and documentation commits into one logical unit.
Done. I've squashed everything into one commit labeled 'Fix blueprint template_folder resolution for absolute paths'. It looks much cleaner in the git log now.
That is perfect. A clean commit history is often the final hurdle before a core maintainer hits that 'Merge' button. The PR looks very professional now.
Wait, I just got a notification from 'GitHub Actions' that one of the older tests in 'tests/test_basic.py' is failing after the rebase. That's unexpected!
Don't panic. Check the diff in 'flask/templating.py'. It's possible the rebase slightly altered the logic or that a stale virtual environment is causing a conflict with the test cache.
Looking at 'tests/test_basic.py' failure, it seems my logic change in 'flask/blueprints.py' had a side effect on how global templates are registered. I need to scope the logic more tightly.
You are right. Ensure that the 'template_folder' modification only triggers if the blueprint is active. Check the conditions in 'flask/templating.py' where the loader is initialized.
I found it. I was modifying the global template loader list even when the blueprint wasn't being evaluated. I'll wrap the logic in a conditional check that looks at the current request context.

Exactly. Use 'flask.globals.request' or 'has_request_context()' to ensure the path injection only happens when the blueprint is actually handling a request. This will prevent polluting the global template environment.
That did the trick! The failure in 'tests/test_basic.py' is resolved, and all my new tests in 'tests/test_blueprints.py' still pass. The fix feels much safer now.
Excellent debugging. By narrowing the scope of the template folder lookup, you've ensured that this change won't negatively impact other parts of the framework.
I'm rerunning all tests now using 'tox'. If this passes, I'm confident in the solution. It's been a long journey from the original 'TemplateNotFound' error.
Tox is the ultimate test. If it completes across all configured environments, you've successfully verified compatibility across Python versions. You're doing great.
Everything passed! The CI environment is green. I'm finalizing the PR description now to summarize the fix, the testing approach, and the documentation update.
Congratulations on reaching this point. Your thorough approach—from isolating the issue to ensuring backward compatibility—is exactly what maintainers want to see. Well done!

I'm reviewing the changes in 'flask/templating.py' one last time before pushing. Does it make sense to add a deprecation warning if a user relies on the old behavior where multiple templates with the same name existed?

That is a thoughtful consideration. However, since the current behavior was arguably a bug in blueprint scoping, a warning might be noisy. Stick to the current fix and focus on documenting the change in 'docs/changes.rst' instead.

Fair point. I'll update 'docs/changes.rst' to clearly state that 'render_template' now prioritizes the blueprint-specific folder if one is defined. Should I also update the API docs in 'flask/blueprints.py'?

Yes, updating the docstring for 'Blueprint' class, specifically the 'template_folder' parameter description, will help future users understand this improved behavior immediately without digging into release notes.
I've updated the docstring. It now explicitly mentions the search precedence. I'm going to run 'make docs' to ensure the Sphinx build doesn't throw any warnings regarding my changes.
Good call. Sphinx is sensitive to formatting. If it compiles cleanly, your documentation change is ready for the PR. Have you verified the 'render_template_string' function as well?
I checked 'flask/templating.py' for 'render_template_string'. It uses a different loader path since it doesn't rely on file paths, so it should be unaffected by my changes to the blueprint loader.
Correct, 'render_template_string' does not interact with the template search path in the same way. Your focus on 'render_template' and 'render_template_defined' is appropriate here.
I'm preparing the final commit. I'll split it into two: one for the core logic in 'flask/templating.py' and one for the tests in 'tests/test_blueprints.py'. Does that sound right?
That is a great practice. Atomic commits make it much easier for maintainers to review your logic versus the verification suite. You are ready to push.
I just pushed the commits to my fork. Should I squash these into a single PR commit before requesting the formal review on GitHub?
Actually, keeping the logic and tests separate is often preferred. Just ensure your commit messages are descriptive. Reference the issue #1361 in both.
Done. Both commits reference #1361. I feel like this really resolves the ambiguity users faced with overlapping template names in Flask applications.
It definitely does. You have improved the predictability of the framework. If someone needs the old behavior, they can always register custom loaders, but this is the correct default.
Looking back at my initial confusion in 'test.py', it’s satisfying to see the test pass now. The framework feels more intuitive after this fix.
That is the hallmark of a great contribution. You addressed an actual pain point that users were encountering. The 'Flask' ecosystem is better for it.
Thanks for all the help with the 'Jinja2' loader logic. I definitely learned a lot about how 'Flask' handles request contexts during template resolution.
You are very welcome. Understanding 'request_context' and 'template_folder' registration is crucial for advanced 'Flask' development. You have mastered a tricky piece of the codebase.
I'm going to monitor the PR for any feedback. If the maintainers request changes, I'll be sure to apply them carefully as we discussed.
That sounds like a solid plan. Good luck with the PR! You have done excellent work on this issue. Reach out if you need any further guidance.

Hey, I just got a ping on the PR. One of the maintainers pointed out that while my fix works for blueprints, it might introduce a performance regression for large applications with many blueprints. They mentioned specifically the 'jinja2.ChoiceLoader' overhead when searching templates. Should I be worried about this?

That is a valid concern in 'flask.templating'. If you are wrapping every single template search in a new 'ChoiceLoader' instance per request, it could add latency. You might want to look at how 'flask.app.Flask' initializes the 'jinja_loader' in 'flask/app.py' and see if we can cache the results of the blueprint lookup.

I see. In my current implementation inside 'flask/templating.py', I am indeed recreating the loader every time 'render_template' is called. If I move that resolution logic into a memoized helper, I could mitigate the overhead significantly. Is that a common pattern in the repo?

Yes, look at 'flask/helpers.py' for similar caching strategies. Using 'functools.lru_cache' on the lookup function would be a clean way to handle this. It will prevent redundant filesystem stats, especially in production environments where templates are rarely added at runtime.

That sounds perfect. I will modify 'flask/templating.py' to include an internal helper function for resolving the blueprint template paths and apply 'lru_cache' there. I should also check if this affects the 'template_folder' property access.

Remember that 'blueprint.template_folder' might change if someone modifies it at runtime, though that is rare. Ensure your cache keys include the app or blueprint instance ID to avoid stale lookups if the application configuration happens to be reloaded.
Good catch. I'll use the blueprint's object ID as part of the key. Let me start refactoring the code. Should I create a new utility module for this, or keep it inside 'flask/templating.py'?

Keep it in 'flask/templating.py'. Flask prefers to keep related logic encapsulated within the module it services. It avoids circular imports and keeps the codebase easier to navigate for other contributors.
